'''Kenneth Norman Kamrin''' is an [[Americans|American]] [[Applied mathematician|Applied Mathematician]] and [[Mechanical engineering|Mechanical Engineer]]. He serves as the Chair of Engineering Science and Professor of Mechanical Engineering at [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California Berkeley]]. 

Kamrin’s research focuses on [[Constitutive equation|constitutive modeling]] and [[computational mechanics]] for large deformation processes spanning elastic and plastic solid [[Model|modeling]], [[Granular material|granular mechanics]], [[Amorphous solid|amorphous]] [[solid mechanics]], and [[Fluid–structure interaction|fluid-structure interaction]]. 

== Education ==
Kamrin received a BS in [[engineering physics]] with a minor in [[mathematics]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California Berkeley]] in 2003<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kamrin |first=Ken |title=Ken Kamrin CV |url=https://web.mit.edu/kkamrin/www/Kamrin_CV.pdf |website=MIT}}</ref>. Kamrin received his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in [[applied mathematics]] from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) in 2008 for his work on stochastic and deterministic models for dense granular flows with [[Martin Z. Bazant|Martin Bazant]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kamrin |first=Kenneth |date=June 2008 |title=Stochastic and Deterministic Models for Dense Granular Flow |url=https://web.mit.edu/kkamrin/www/main.pdf}}</ref>.

== Academic Career ==
Kamrin began his academic career as an [[applied mathematics]] lecturer and [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] Postdoctoral Fellow in the School of Engineering and Applied Sciences at [[Harvard University]] in 2008. Kamrin joined the faculty of the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in the [[Mechanical engineering|Mechanical Engineering department]] in 2011, where he later served as the Class of 1956 Career Development Chair and also received a second faculty appointment in [[Applied mathematics|Applied Mathematics]]. After serving as a professor at MIT for 13 years, Kamrin joined the [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California Berkeley]] as a Mechanical Engineering professor in 2024<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ken Kamrin {{!}} Research UC Berkeley |url=https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/ken-kamrin |access-date=2026-09-20 |website=vcresearch.berkeley.edu}}</ref> where he was appointed the Chair of [[Engineering Science]] in 2025.   

A performer by upbringing in a musical theater family, Kamrin is a sought-after teacher and speaker on the subject of mechanics. He has provided commentary for the [[National Geographic (American TV channel)|National Geographic channel]]<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sFbIry9UYG8 |title=Monster Plane: Uncovering the Antonov AN-255 (Full Episode) {{!}} Superstructures: Engineering Marvels |date=2024-10-12 |last=National Geographic |access-date=2026-09-22 |via=YouTube}}</ref>[[National Geographic (American TV channel)|,]] was the subject of a New-England-Emmy nominated film on granular media<ref>Documentary Orator for "The Nature of sand". [https://newenglandemmy.org/files/2019/04/2019-New-England-Nominations.pdf 2018 New England Emmy Award Nomination]</ref><ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8xAfzz1HT8s |title=The Nature of Sand |date=2018-05-11 |last=MIT Mechanical Engineering |access-date=2026-09-22 |via=YouTube}}</ref>, and gave the 10-university [https://sites.google.com/iit.edu/mms/home Midwest Mechanics Seminar] tour in 2025<ref>{{Cite web |title=MMS |url=https://sites.google.com/iit.edu/mms/home |access-date=2026-09-20 |website=sites.google.com |language=en-US}}</ref>. Kamrin received MIT's highest honor in undergraduate education, the [[Margaret MacVicar|MacVicar Fellowship]], in 2022.  

== Research ==
Kamrin's research focuses on [[continuum mechanics]] and the modeling of [[Granular material|granular]], [[Continuum mechanics|deformable]], and [[Multiphase flow|multiphase]] materials. His work combines [[Constitutive equation|constitutive]] modeling, [[theoretical mechanics]], and [[Computational engineering|computational methods]] to relate microscopic material behavior to macroscopic deformation and flow.<ref>{{cite web |date=27 March 2019 |title=Professor Ken Kamrin |url=https://news.mit.edu/2019/professor-ken-kamrin-0327 |website=MIT News}}</ref>

A major area of his research is [[Granular material|granular rheology]]. Kamrin has developed non-local continuum models for dense granular flow that incorporate finite spatial interactions into constitutive descriptions<ref name=":2" />. These models have been used to describe many different flow regimes, including localized deformation and transitions between flowing and arrested states. His research has also examined the effects of particle size and characteristic length scales on granular rheology and the scaling of granular behavior across different flow geometries<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" />. Kamrin has investigated continuum models for systems containing interacting granular and fluid phases, including [[Slurry|fluid–sediment]] mixtures and non-Newtonian fine-particle suspensions. These [[Two-phase flow|multi-phase models]] treat the constituent phases as coupled continua and seek to describe multiple regimes of [[Sediment transport|particulate transport]] within a common framework<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":6" />. Another area of his research concerns the mechanics of solid objects moving through granular materials<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite journal |first1=Shashank |date=1 October 2019 |title=Modeling of the interaction of rigid wheels with dry granular media |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022489818302064 |journal=Journal of Terramechanics |volume=85 |pages=1–14|last1=Agarwal|last2=Senatore|first2=Carmine|last3=Zhang|first3=Tingnan|last4=Kingsbury|first4=Mark|last5=Iagnemma|first5=Karl|last6=Goldman|first6=Daniel|first7=Ken|last7=Kamrin |doi=10.1016/j.jterra.2019.06.001 |bibcode=2019JTerr..85....1A }}</ref>. His work on granular intrusion has examined the forces acting on bodies moving through granular media and developed reduced descriptions of these forces. Related studies have considered [[locomotion]] in granular materials, [[terramechanics]], and the interaction between moving bodies and granular terrains on earth and beyond<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":7" />.

Kamrin has also developed [[Computational methods in engineering|computational methods]] for materials undergoing large deformation, including the Reference Map Technique<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |first1=Ken |date=30 November 2011 |title=Reference map technique for finite-strain elasticity and fluid–solid interaction |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022509612001135 |journal=Journal of the Mechanics and Physics of Solids |volume=60 |issue=11 |pages=1952–1969|last1=Kamrin|first2=Chris H|last2=Rycroft|last3=Nave|first3=Jean-Christophe |doi=10.1016/j.jmps.2012.06.003 }}</ref> for [[Finite element method|finite-deformation mechanics]] and methods coupling [[Discrete element method|discrete]] and [[Continuum mechanics|continuum]] descriptions of particulate materials<ref name=":1" />. A recurring theme of this work is the development of continuum and reduced-order models that capture [[Macroscopic scale|macroscopic]] material behavior without requiring all [[Microscopic scale|microscopic]] degrees of freedom to be explicitly resolved.
